questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: He is waiting in the bus stop.
She went out the door and into the garden.
The car drove beside the river slowly.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: You wait at a bus stop, not "in the bus stop," since you are not inside it. The prepositions in "beside the river" and "out the door and into the garden" are both fine.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The childrens' toys were scattered everywhere.
The women's coats were hanging by the door.
The child's toy was missing from the shelf.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: The word "children" is already plural, so the possessive is "children's toys," not "childrens' toys." The forms "child's" and "women's" are both built correctly.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The cat slept under the bed during the storm.
She placed the book beside the laptop.
He waited in line for almost an hour.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three sentences are fine, so choose "No mistakes." The prepositions "under the bed," "beside the laptop" and "in line" all fit, and every verb matches its subject.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The cake tasted delicious after it was baked.
The athlete performed wonderfully at the competition.
He drove very slow on the icy road.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: A verb needs an adverb, so "drove very slow" should be "drove very slowly." The adverb "wonderfully" and the adjective "delicious" after the linking verb "tasted" are both correct.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The coach handed out new jerseys before Friday's game.
Two of the windows in the art room stick when it rains.
Our cousins arrived an hour before the parade started.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three sentences are correct, so (No mistakes) is the answer. Friday's is a correct possessive and the verb tenses agree with the time words in each sentence.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The student's books were left on the table.
The children's playground is closed today.
The teachers lounge is down the hall.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: A possessive noun needs an apostrophe, so "The teachers lounge" should be "The teachers' lounge." The forms "student's" and "children's" are punctuated correctly.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The wind blew through the trees all night.
The teacher had taught us the lesson by then.
He drove to the office early this morning.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three sentences are fine, so choose "No mistakes." "Blew" is the past tense of blow, "had taught" shows an action finished before "then," and "drove" matches "this morning."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The teacher asked, "Did you finish your homework"?
I have three things to do today: clean, cook, and study.
The dog ran outside without his leash!
No mistakes
questions.explanation: In "Did you finish your homework"? the question mark belongs inside the quotation marks, because the question is part of what the teacher actually said.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: We're planning to visit three cities: Paris, London, and Berlin.
I enjoy hiking in the mountains; it's relaxing.
I love running and biking, those are my favorite sports.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "I love running and biking, those are my favorite sports" joins two complete sentences with only a comma. Use a semicolon or a period instead of that comma.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: We need the following items: paper, pens, and tape.
The dinner was delicious; I had seconds.
We need to buy groceries, do laundry, and cook dinner.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. The colon introduces a list, the semicolon joins two complete sentences and the commas separate the items in a series.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: He asked, "Where did you find that?"
The teacher asked, "Did you submit your assignment?"
She asked if I was going to the party?
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "She asked if I was going to the party?" only tells about a question, so it should end with a period. Use a question mark only when the sentence itself asks something.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: I think we should go; it's getting late.
We traveled to Spain; the beaches were beautiful.
The movie starts at 8:00, and we'll be late.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. Both semicolons join two complete sentences, and the comma before "and" in "The movie starts at 8:00, and we'll be late." is exactly right.

questions.stem: Topic: The advantages of learning to play a musical instrument. Which sentence least supports the topic?
options: Musicians often develop better coordination and discipline.
Playing music can be a form of stress relief and emotional expression.
Some instruments are more expensive than others.
Learning an instrument can improve cognitive skills and memory.
questions.explanation: The odd sentence is the one that does not support the topic. Better thinking, stress relief and coordination are all advantages of playing music, while the cost of instruments is about price, not benefits.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence that best expresses the idea most clearly.
options: Because of their enjoyment, the audience was enthusiastic in their applause.
The audience applauded enthusiastically because they enjoyed the performance.
Enthusiastically applauding, the audience enjoyed the performance.
The performance was enjoyed by the audience who applauded enthusiastically.
questions.explanation: Clear writing puts the doer first and states the cause plainly. 'The audience applauded enthusiastically because they enjoyed the performance' does both, while the other choices use passive wording or rearrange the idea awkwardly.

questions.stem: Select the sentence that best expresses the idea clearly.
options: She baked the cake in the kitchen yesterday.
Yesterday, the kitchen was where the cake was baked by her.
In the kitchen yesterday, the cake was baked.
The cake was baked by her in the kitchen yesterday.
questions.explanation: Active voice, with the doer first, is usually the clearest. 'She baked the cake in the kitchen yesterday' names who did the action, while the passive versions bury her behind 'was baked by.'

questions.stem: Choose the best word to join the sentences. 'I wanted to go for a walk. It was raining heavily.'
options: because
and
so
but
questions.explanation: This asks for the joining word that shows how the two ideas relate. Wanting a walk and heavy rain clash, so 'but' shows that contrast, while 'so' and 'because' would wrongly signal cause.

questions.stem: Select the word that best connects the sentences. 'She studied hard for the test. She earned a high score.'
options: Therefore
Although
However
Meanwhile
questions.explanation: Decide what the second sentence does to the first. Studying hard led to the high score, so 'Therefore' shows a result, while 'However' would signal a contrast that is not there.

questions.stem: Choose the best word to complete the sentence. 'He didn't see the stop sign, ______ he got a traffic ticket.'
options: yet
because
so
unless
questions.explanation: The connector must match the relationship between the two clauses. Missing the stop sign caused the ticket, so 'so' shows the result, while 'because' would reverse the cause and the effect.

questions.stem: Choose the best word to join the sentences. 'He was tired, ______ he continued working.'
options: therefore
but
because
so
questions.explanation: Being tired and continuing to work do not match, so the joining word must show contrast. 'But' does that, while 'so' and 'therefore' would say being tired caused him to keep working.

questions.stem: Select the word that best connects the sentences. 'The team practiced every day. They won the championship.'
options: However
Meanwhile
Consequently
Because
questions.explanation: Daily practice led to the championship, so the connector should show a result. 'Consequently' means as a result, while 'However' signals contrast and 'Meanwhile' signals time.

questions.stem: Identify the sentence that does not fit in the following paragraph.
options: The invention of the printing press revolutionized the spread of information.
Before its invention, books were copied by hand, which was a slow process.
The printing press allowed for mass production of books, making them more accessible.
The internet has also greatly impacted how we access information.
questions.explanation: Find the sentence that is off topic. The paragraph is about the printing press, so hand-copied books and mass production belong, while 'The internet has also greatly impacted how we access information' jumps to modern technology.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The novel Pride and Prejudice is a classic.
We are going to florida for vacation.
My family visited the Grand Canyon last summer.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "florida" is the name of a state, so it needs a capital F. Proper nouns such as states, cities and countries are always capitalized.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The statue of Liberty is located in New York City.
Our teacher assigned a project on the American Revolution.
My favorite book is The Catcher in the Rye.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "statue of Liberty" should be "Statue of Liberty." Every important word in the name of one specific monument gets a capital letter.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: We studied the history of the medieval Period in Europe.
I enjoy reading books by J.K. Rowling.
He lives near the University of Chicago.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "medieval Period" should be "medieval period." A general stretch of time is not capitalized; only named periods, like the Renaissance, get capitals.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The capitol building is located in Washington, D.C.
My favorite sports team is the Los Angeles Lakers.
She read The Hunger Games over the summer.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "capitol building" should be "Capitol Building." It is the name of one specific building in Washington, D.C., so both words take capitals.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: I'm studying World History this semester.
Our family is planning a trip to the Rocky Mountains.
We're going to the beach this Summer.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Seasons are not capitalized, so "this Summer" should be "this summer." "World History" is fine because it names one specific course.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: They're going to visit the Eiffel Tower in France.
My aunt works in the finance department at her company.
We saw a movie called a Beautiful Mind last weekend.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "a Beautiful Mind" should be "A Beautiful Mind." The first word of a title is always capitalized, even when it is a small word like "a."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: We learned about the civil Rights Movement in school.
She works in New York City for a large company.
The Pacific Ocean is the largest ocean on Earth.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "civil Rights Movement" should be "Civil Rights Movement." Named historical events and movements take a capital on every important word.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The book To Kill a Mockingbird is on my reading list.
I'm traveling to the White House next year.
He attends mass every Sunday morning.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "mass" should be "Mass" when it names the Catholic worship service. Names of specific religious services are treated as proper nouns.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: My brother is attending Harvard university next fall.
We studied the Constitution in our government class.
She visited Mount Rushmore with her family last year.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Harvard university" should be "Harvard University." When you name one specific school, the word "University" is part of that name and gets a capital.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: I'm going to the Art Institute of Chicago this weekend.
They're learning about the renaissance in history class.
My sister is studying engineering at Stanford University.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "renaissance" should be "Renaissance" because it names one specific period in history. Notice that "history class" correctly stays lowercase.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: She was inspired by the play Romeo and Juliet.
Our school is visiting the smithsonian museums in Washington.
The Mississippi River flows through several states.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "smithsonian" should be "Smithsonian." It is the name of one specific group of museums, and names are proper nouns that need a capital letter.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The Getty Museum is a popular tourist attraction in Los Angeles.
My friend loves to read about the titanic.
We visited the Empire State Building last summer.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "the titanic" should be "the Titanic." Ships have names, and the name of a specific ship is a proper noun that needs a capital.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The book Of Mice and men was a class favorite.
He's a big fan of the Dallas Cowboys.
We are planning a trip to South Africa in December.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Of Mice and men" should be "Of Mice and Men." In a title you capitalize the main words, and "men" is a noun, not a small joining word.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The Brooklyn Bridge connects Manhattan and Brooklyn.
She's studying the Industrial revolution in her class.
My family attends Mass every Sunday.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Industrial revolution" should be "Industrial Revolution." A named historical event takes a capital on every important word in its name.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: She is reading The Chronicles of Narnia for the first time.
He went to the Museum of Modern Art in New York City.
My parents are going to Italy in the Spring.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Seasons stay lowercase, so "in the Spring" should be "in the spring." Months like December are capitalized, but spring, summer, fall and winter are not.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: My cousin is learning about the Roman Empire.
We visited the Vatican during our trip to Rome.
The book the Great Gatsby is on our reading list.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "the Great Gatsby" should be "The Great Gatsby." The first word of a title is capitalized, even when that word happens to be "the."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The manager approved the project.
She was excited to finaly graduate.
We will definitely go to the concert.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Finaly" should be "finally." Final plus -ly keeps both l's, one from "final" and one from the ending "-ly."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: I accidentaly broke the glass.
They were planning a surprise party.
The teacher appreciated the students' hard work.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Accidentaly" should be "accidentally." Start from the adjective "accidental" and add -ly, which gives you two l's at the end.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: She was a strong competitor in the race.
The hotel had a magnificant view of the beach.
We had to cancel the appointment.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Magnificant" should be "magnificent." This word ends in -ent, the same way "excellent" and "different" do.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The temperature droped overnight.
He always gave great advice to his friends.
I don’t know how to maneuver the new equipment.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Droped" should be "dropped." When a short word ends in one vowel plus one consonant, double that consonant before adding -ed.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: She was given an award for her acheivements.
The children were playing outside in the field.
He had to rewrite his entire essay.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Acheivements" should be "achievements." Use the old rhyme, i before e except after c, to remember that the base word is "achieve."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The cat chased the mouse across the room.
She loves to read historical novels.
The counsil met to discuss the new regulations.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Counsil" should be "council." A council is a group that meets, and it ends in -cil. Do not mix it up with "counsel," which means advice.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The policemen worked together to solve the case.
She had a large collection of jewelry.
The man was convicted of burgulary.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Burgulary" should be "burglary." There is no u after the g; the word is simply "burglar" with a y on the end.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: He always carried a notebook to write down ideas.
They were concerned about the environment.
The sun shone brightly over the horizen.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Horizen" should be "horizon." The last syllable uses an o, which you can hear clearly in the longer word "horizontal."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The patient was recovering after surgery.
He had to apoligize for his mistake.
They lost their way in the labyrinth of streets.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Apoligize" should be "apologize." It comes from "apology," so the middle letter is an o, not an i.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: She organized her closet over the weekend.
The goverment passed new laws to protect wildlife.
The cat knocked over the vase.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Goverment" should be "government." Say it slowly as "govern" plus "-ment" and you will hear the n that is so easy to drop.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The project required a great deal of coordination.
He was an excellent student throughout high school.
The doctor gave a perscription for the medication.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Perscription" should be "prescription." It begins with "pre-," like "prescribe," because the doctor writes the order before you get the medicine.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The company was known for its innovations.
We explored the museum for hours.
She read the instructions before starting the experimant.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Experimant" should be "experiment." The ending is -ment, the same ending you see in "movement" and "argument."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The librarian arranged the schedule for the weekend volunteers.
Our neighbors are grateful for the extra parking spaces.
She wrote the address on the back of the receipt.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Librarian, schedule, grateful and receipt are all spelled correctly, so (No mistakes) is the answer.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: She presented a well-researched report.
He was known for his kindness and generosity.
The comittee voted on the proposal.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Comittee" should be "committee." This word has a double m, a double t and a double e, so think of it as the word with three pairs.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: They have traveled to many countries.
He has ran the marathon three times.
She has written a novel.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: After "has," the verb run uses its past participle "run," not "ran," so it should be "He has run the marathon." The participles "written" and "traveled" are correct.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: She shared the cookies with her friends.
He walked between the two buildings.
Between you and I, I think the test was difficult.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: After a preposition like "between," use an object pronoun, so "Between you and I" should be "Between you and me." The other two sentences are correct as written.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: I feel bad about your situation.
She feels happy today.
He feels sick after eating too much candy.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three sentences are fine, so choose "No mistakes." After a linking verb like feel, you use an adjective, so "feel bad," "feels happy" and "feels sick" are all right.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: He didn't do anything wrong.
She doesn't have any money left.
They don't know anyone at the party.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three sentences are fine, so choose "No mistakes." Each one uses a single negative paired with "anything," "any" or "anyone," so none of them doubles its negatives.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Each of the books is on the shelf.
Every one of the books is on the shelf.
All of the books are on the shelf.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three sentences are fine, so choose "No mistakes." "Each" and "every one" are singular and take "is," while "all of the books" is plural and takes "are."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Whose jacket is this?
Who's bringing the snacks?
Whose going to the game tonight?
No mistakes
questions.explanation: The word "whose" shows possession and "who's" means "who is," so "Whose going to the game" should be "Who's going." "Who's bringing" and "Whose jacket" are both right.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: If I were taller, I could reach the shelf.
If she were here, she would help us.
If they were ready, we could start.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three sentences are fine, so choose "No mistakes." For an imagined or untrue situation, English uses "were" with every subject, so "If I were" and "If she were" are right.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: They wondered where their friends had gone.
He didn't know where he was at.
She asked where the library was.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: The word "at" is not needed after "where," so "where he was at" should be "where he was." The other two sentences end their where-clauses correctly.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Our science class visited the water treatment plant.
The mail carrier leaves the packages by the side door.
I need to lay down for a while.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Lay takes an object, so a person lies down. The sentence should read "I need to lie down for a while."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The number of participants is increasing.
There are a number of reasons why we should go.
A large amount of people attended the event.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Use "number" for things you can count and "amount" for things you cannot, so "A large amount of people" should be "a large number of people." The other two sentences are fine.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: He is the eldest of the two brothers.
She keeps a spare house key in her jacket pocket.
The hardware store on Third Street opens at six.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: The superlative eldest is used for three or more. With only two brothers the comparative is correct: "the elder of the two brothers."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: He labeled each box before loading the truck.
She sat the vase on the shelf.
The rain finally stopped just before the second half.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Sat cannot take an object. Placing something somewhere calls for set: "She set the vase on the shelf."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The mechanic explained the repair twice before we understood it.
The box of faded photographs and letters were stored in the attic.
Our flight lands a little after midnight.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: The subject is "box," which is singular, so the verb should be "was stored." The phrase "of faded photographs and letters" sits between the subject and the verb but does not change its number.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: He folded the map and slid it into his pocket.
The trail ended at a shallow creek lined with willows.
Neither of the two explanations make sense to me.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Neither" is a singular indefinite pronoun, so it takes "makes." The plural noun in the phrase "of the two explanations" does not control the verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The gym was packed, we found two seats in the last row.
The bus pulled away before Danny reached the corner.
Our coach handed out the new jerseys after warm-ups.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: This is a comma splice: two complete sentences joined by only a comma. It needs a period, a semicolon or a comma plus "so."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Her office is on the third floor of the courthouse.
My aunt teaches at a High School just outside Denver.
We drove past two horse farms on the way there.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "High school" is a common noun here and should be lowercase. It is capitalized only when it is part of an actual name, such as Regis Jesuit High School.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Neither of the boys is willing to apologize first.
The hikers rested at the summit for almost an hour.
My sister enjoys cooking more than I do.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. "Neither" is singular, so "is" is right even though "boys" is plural, and "more than I do" correctly uses the subject pronoun.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: She rewrote the opening paragraph three times.
The gym smelled like fresh paint on the first day of school.
Neither the coach nor the players was ready for the schedule change.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: With "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. "Players" is plural, so the verb should be "were."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The recipe looked simple, however, it took us three hours.
She keeps a spare key taped under the mailbox.
We hiked to the ridge and ate lunch under a pine.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "However" is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot join two sentences with commas. Use a semicolon before it: "simple; however, it took..."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: She left her badge on the kitchen counter.
The gym floor was refinished over the break.
Our class interviewed Principal Novak and then the Superintendent.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: A title is capitalized when it comes directly before a name, as in "Principal Novak," but lowercase when it stands alone as an office: "the superintendent."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Mrs. Whitfield handed the permission slips to Jamal and I.
He practiced the same three chords all afternoon.
The bus was already full when we reached the corner.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "To" is a preposition, so it takes the object pronoun: "to Jamal and me." Dropping the other name makes the error easy to hear.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: A thin layer of frost covered the windshield.
Please send the completed forms to Mr. Ortiz or myself.
The sprinklers came on while we were still eating lunch.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Myself" is a reflexive pronoun and can only be used when the subject is "I." The correct object pronoun here is "me."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The concert ended a few minutes past ten.
My cousin drove us to the airport in the rain.
After the long ride through the canyon in the back of the truck we were ready for lunch.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: A long introductory phrase must be followed by a comma: "...in the back of the truck, we were ready for lunch."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Each of the guest rooms has their own thermostat.
She reads two chapters every night before bed.
The freight elevator opens onto the loading dock.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Each" is singular, which the verb "has" already shows, so the pronoun must be singular too: "its own thermostat."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The coach whom the players trusted retired in June.
Every one of the windows was left open during the storm.
We waited under the awning until the rain let up.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. "Whom" is right because it is the object of "trusted," and "Every one...was" is singular even though "windows" is plural.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Mr. Delgado who teaches biology also coaches the tennis team.
We hung the calendar on the back of the pantry door.
The sprinkler soaked the sidewalk and half the driveway.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: The clause "who teaches biology" adds extra information about a person already identified by name, so it must be set off with commas on both sides.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The ferry runs every hour until sunset.
My grandparents moved to the south after they retired.
He packed two sweaters and a rain jacket.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Used as the name of a region, "the South" is capitalized. Only a direction stays lowercase, as in "drove south for an hour."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The puppy chewed a hole in the corner of the rug.
By the time we reached the theater, the movie already started.
We repainted the shed last weekend.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: When one past action happens before another, the earlier one takes the past perfect: "the movie had already started."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The wind rattled the shutters most of the night.
Both of my parent's cars need new tires before winter.
He kept the receipt in the glove compartment.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Both" shows there are two parents, so the apostrophe belongs after the s: "my parents' cars."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Next year I will take algebra, french and world history.
He rides his bike to school when the weather is clear.
The cafeteria serves breakfast until eight.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: The name of a language is always capitalized, so it should be French. Ordinary school subjects such as algebra and world history stay lowercase unless they name a specific course.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Last Tuesday Marisol told me that she will bring the poster board.
The garden hose froze solid overnight.
Every player signed the banner before the bus left.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: When the reporting verb is past tense ("told"), the verb in the reported clause shifts back too: "that she would bring the poster board."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The Ramirezes' driveway was repaved last week.
We arrived early; the doors were already unlocked.
She asked whether the museum is open on Mondays.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. The plural family name Ramirezes takes only an apostrophe, the semicolon joins two complete sentences, and the last sentence reports a question rather than asking one, so it ends with a period.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The library stays open an extra hour during exam week.
If we had left ten minutes earlier, we would of missed the storm.
He carried the ladder around to the back of the house.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Would of" is a misspelling of the contraction "would've." The correct form is "would have missed."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: A moth kept circling the porch light.
The bell rang twice before anyone moved.
The gray backpack by the door is her's.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe. The word is "hers," just as we write ours, yours and theirs.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: We borrowed a projector from the media center.
Our class watched a documentary called "Life In The Deep Ocean."
The rain washed the chalk off the sidewalk.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: In a title, short prepositions and articles inside the title stay lowercase: "Life in the Deep Ocean." Only the first word, the last word and the important words are capitalized.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: She taped the schedule to the inside of her locker.
Of the three routes to the stadium, the one along the river is shorter.
A hawk circled above the empty parking lot.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: The comparative "shorter" compares only two things. Comparing three routes calls for the superlative: "is the shortest."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: He lay on the couch for an hour after the game.
The package arrived sooner than we expected.
Our neighbors painted their front porch a bright yellow.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. "Lay" looks like an error but is the correct past tense of "lie," meaning to recline, and "their" correctly matches the plural "neighbors."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The road curved sharply and then dropped into the valley.
Nora finished her essay well before dinner.
We packed the essentials; a tent, a lantern and a first-aid kit.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: A list introduced by a complete statement takes a colon, not a semicolon. A semicolon is used only between two complete sentences.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: She saved the program from the spring recital.
The band marched twice around the track.
The choir sang "america the Beautiful" at the assembly.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: The first word of a title is always capitalized, so it should be "America the Beautiful." The small word "the" inside the title correctly stays lowercase.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Our neighbors adopted a gray cat with one white paw.
The kitchen faucet has dripped since August.
The directions on the second page are more simpler than the ones on the first.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Simpler" is already a comparative, so adding "more" doubles it. Write either "simpler than" or "more straightforward than."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: We split the last piece of cornbread.
The dog barked at the recycling truck every Tuesday.
Although the sky was completely clear; the wind made the field feel freezing.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins two complete sentences, but "Although the sky was completely clear" cannot stand alone. It needs a comma instead.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The train pulled out of the station right on time.
The soup on the back burner smells wonderfully.
He borrowed a pen from the girl beside him.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Smells" is a linking verb here, so it is followed by an adjective describing the soup: "smells wonderful."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: My dad drinks a cup of coffee and a can of coke every afternoon.
We bought paper plates for the picnic.
The vending machine takes only dollar bills.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Coke is a brand name and must be capitalized, while a general product such as coffee stays lowercase.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Mr. Alvarez gave the extra tickets to my brother and me.
The bus had already left by the time we reached the corner.
Only one of the puppies was still awake.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. "Me" is the right object pronoun after "to," the past perfect "had left" marks the earlier action, and "one...was" is singular.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: She left her water bottle on the bleachers.
A row of tall hedges hides the fence from the street.
The team either practices in the gym or on the back field.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Correlative conjunctions must join matching parts. "Either" belongs after the verb so the two phrases match: "practices either in the gym or on the back field."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: A hummingbird hovered by the feeder for a moment.
Ms. Ibarra called my draft "thoughtful and unusually clear".
The librarian renewed my book for another two weeks.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: In American usage a period always goes inside the closing quotation mark: "unusually clear."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: I asked mom whether I could stay after school for practice.
The recycling bin was already at the curb.
The porch swing creaks whenever the wind picks up.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: When a family word is used in place of a name, it is capitalized: "I asked Mom." It stays lowercase only after a possessive, as in "my mom."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: He returned the library book two days late.
Walking home from practice, the streetlights flickered on one by one.
The bread cooled on a rack near the window.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: An opening participial phrase must describe the subject that follows it. As written, the streetlights are walking home from practice.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The judges' scores were posted online Friday night.
After the ceremony finally ended, we walked to the diner.
He said, "The last train leaves at six."
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. "Judges'" is a proper plural possessive, the introductory clause is followed by a comma, and the period sits inside the quotation marks.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The twins repaired the bike chain theirselves.
The clock in the kitchen runs about five minutes fast.
She stacked the folding chairs against the wall.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Theirselves is not a standard word. The reflexive pronoun is themselves.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Could you tell me which hallway the auditorium is on.
The rain finally let up around four o'clock.
He left his cleats in the back of the car.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: This is a real question addressed to someone, so it must end with a question mark, not a period.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The elevator stops on every floor of the hospital.
We planted three rows of carrots along the fence.
Our new neighbor speaks portuguese at home.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Names of languages are proper nouns and are always capitalized: Portuguese.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Two crows landed on the fence post.
The new bus schedule had a noticeable affect on attendance.
We hung the poster above the water fountain.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: The noun meaning result is "effect." "Affect" is almost always the verb, meaning to influence.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: She turned in a well written report on the water cycle.
The lights in the hallway buzz when it rains.
The trail loops around the pond and back to the parking lot.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: A compound modifier placed before the noun it describes is hyphenated: "a well-written report."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Each of the twins has a different favorite color.
We could not find anyone who knew the way to the trailhead.
The reason she left early was that her ride showed up.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. "Each...has" is singular even with "twins" nearby, and "The reason...was that" is the standard form, not "was because."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The gate at the end of the driveway sticks in wet weather.
He tightened the loose screw on the cabinet door.
The line at the bakery was longer then it was last Saturday.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Than" makes a comparison; "then" refers to time. The sentence compares two lines, so it needs "longer than."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: It's been a long week for everyone on the crew.
My uncle, who restores old radios, gave me one for my birthday.
Bring a jacket, a hat and sturdy boots.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. "It's" is the contraction of "it has," the extra information about the uncle is correctly set off by a pair of commas, and no comma is needed before "and" in the short list.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The old clock in the hallway lost it's minute hand years ago.
The museum offers a free tour on the first Sunday of the month.
We carried the folding table out to the yard.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: The possessive form is "its," with no apostrophe. "It's" always means "it is" or "it has."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: We found the missing glove under the bleachers.
The rain stopped a little after noon but the field was still too muddy to play on.
The kettle whistled from the back of the stove.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: When a coordinating conjunction such as "but" joins two complete sentences, a comma goes before it: "...after noon, but the field..."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The parade starts at the corner of Fifth and Elm.
We repainted the mailbox a deep green.
Our whole family gathers every thanksgiving at my aunt's house.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Holidays are proper nouns and are capitalized: Thanksgiving.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Let me know when your ready to head out to the field.
She wrote the address on the back of an envelope.
The pond behind the school freezes by early January.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "You're" is the contraction of "you are," which is what the sentence means. "Your" shows possession.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Our team practices on the field behind the middle school.
The boy standing near the water fountain, waved at us.
She taped a note to the refrigerator.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: A single comma should never separate a subject from its verb. The comma after "fountain" has to go.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Aunt Rita drove us to the Denver Museum of Nature and Science.
In the fall, my brother starts classes at Creighton University.
We read a poem by Langston Hughes in English class.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. "Aunt Rita" is a title used with a name, seasons such as "fall" are lowercase, and "English" is capitalized because it is a language.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: There were less students in the hallway after the late bell.
The bell rang while we were still packing up.
He hung his jacket on the hook by the door.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Use "fewer" for things you can count, such as students, and "less" for amounts you cannot count, such as noise or time.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The truck backed slowly into the narrow alley.
Please hand me the smaller wrench Marcus.
A row of lockers lines the west wall.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: A name used to address someone directly is set off with a comma: "the smaller wrench, Marcus."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The prize money was divided between the seven finalists.
The choir rehearses in the band room on Thursdays.
A thin crack ran the length of the windshield.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Between" is used for two; with more than two, use "among the seven finalists."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a punctuation mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Ms. O'Donnell's class visited the planetarium on Tuesday.
We could not decide between the two routes, so we flipped a coin.
Did anyone remember to lock the back door?
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. The apostrophe in O'Donnell belongs to the name and the possessive s is added normally, a comma correctly precedes "so" joining two sentences, and the direct question ends with a question mark.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: We stacked the firewood behind the garage.
The porch light burned out sometime last night.
Everyone in my family excepted the invitation to the reunion.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "Accept" means to receive or agree to; "except" means to leave out. The sentence needs "accepted."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: I have never been good at these kind of puzzles.
He set his alarm for five in the morning.
The batteries in the smoke detector need to be replaced.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: "These" is plural and "kind" is singular, so they do not match. Write "this kind of puzzle" or "these kinds of puzzles."

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Whom did the principal choose to speak at the assembly?
We had hoped to leave before dark, but the storm delayed us.
A pair of gloves was left on the bench outside the gym.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. "Whom" is the object of "choose," and "A pair...was" is singular even though "gloves" is plural.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a capitalization mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: My mom studied Spanish and chemistry at a small college in Iowa.
The ferry crosses Lake Michigan twice a day in the summer.
Uncle Devon lives just north of the airport.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. "My mom" follows a possessive so it stays lowercase, a language is capitalized while chemistry is not, and "north" here is a direction rather than a region.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a mistake in grammar or usage? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: A stack of yearbooks sat on the counter by the office.
The counselor who we met at orientation is retiring in June.
The rain stopped just before the ceremony began.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: The pronoun is the object of "met," so the correct form is "whom we met at orientation." Use "who" only when the pronoun is the subject of its own clause.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The bus driver waved to us as she pulled away.
Our neighbor keeps a canoe in his garage all winter.
The judges recieved more than 90 entries in the poetry contest.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Recieved should be received. The i-before-e rule reverses after c, so the e comes first.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The lake freezes solid by the middle of January.
Please keep the wet towels seperate from the clean ones.
My uncle repairs clocks in a shop on Ninth Street.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Seperate should be separate. The unstressed middle vowel sounds like a short uh, but it is spelled with an a.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Marcus is definately planning to try out for the play.
She left her gloves on the bench near the field.
The library closes an hour early on Fridays.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Definately should be definitely. The word is built on finite, so the middle vowel is an i.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The first occurence of the word appears on page 12.
Our science teacher grew up on a farm in Nebraska.
He folded the map and put it in his back pocket.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Occurence should be occurrence. Adding the ending to occur doubles the r.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The choir practices in the auditorium on Tuesday evenings.
A permit is neccessary before anyone can build a shed.
Rain fell steadily through the whole parade.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Neccessary should be necessary, which has one c and two s's, not the reverse.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The calender on the refrigerator still shows last month.
Two of my cousins live within walking distance.
He carried the groceries up three flights of stairs.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Calender should be calendar. The last vowel is an a even though it sounds like a short uh.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Her older brother works nights at the hospital.
The forecast promised sun for the whole weekend.
Nobody could prove the existance of the tunnel under the school.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Existance should be existence. Verbs ending in -ist usually take -ence rather than -ance.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Anna clapped along with the rythm of the song.
We packed sandwiches for the drive to the coast.
The drummer counted off the first measure.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Rythm should be rhythm. The silent h after the r is easy to leave out because it is not heard.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The coach called a timeout with 30 seconds left.
It would embarass him to be praised in front of everyone.
My grandmother still writes letters by hand.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Embarass should be embarrass, which doubles both the r and the s.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The trail follows the river for almost four miles.
The patient was concious the entire time.
We repainted the porch railing last spring.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Concious should be conscious. The sh sound is spelled sci, so the s before the c is needed.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Driving is a priviledge, not a right.
The dog barked at the mail carrier again.
Every ticket includes a program and a bottle of water.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Priviledge should be privilege. There is no d in the word, even though it sounds like the ending of knowledge.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The store opens at ten on Sunday mornings.
Todd was dissapointed when the trip was canceled.
My aunt planted tulips along the front walk.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Dissapointed should be disappointed. The prefix dis- joins appoint, so the s is single and the p is doubled.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The tomatoes ripened faster than we expected.
He borrowed a ladder from the family next door.
The landlord is responsible for the maintainance of the roof.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Maintainance should be maintenance. The noun drops the i of maintain.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Her perseverence finally earned her a place on the team.
She reads the newspaper before anyone else is awake.
Only one lane of the highway was open.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Perseverence should be perseverance. The ending is -ance, matching persevere plus -ance.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: We stacked the firewood against the fence.
The kitten hid behind the washing machine for hours.
He wore his father's watch only on one occassion.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Occassion should be occasion, which doubles the c but not the s.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: Snow covered the picnic tables by morning.
Several atheletes signed up for the summer clinic.
The mechanic said the repair would take two days.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: Atheletes should be athletes. Many people say the word with an extra syllable, but no vowel belongs between the h and the l.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The twins were too mischievous to leave alone in the kitchen.
A weird humming came from behind the vending machine.
She scrubbed the stain until it was barely noticeable.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. Mischievous has no i before the final ous, weird is one of the words that breaks the i-before-e rule and noticeable keeps the e of notice to hold the soft c.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: We ate at a restaurant two blocks from the theater.
The old cemetery sits on a hill above the town.
His conscience bothered him for a week afterward.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. Cemetery is spelled with three e's and no a, and conscience ends in -science even though it is not pronounced that way.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The committee meets separately from the full council.
Rhythm and balance matter more than speed in this routine.
She definitely intends to apply for the scholarship.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. These are the standard spellings of three of the most commonly misspelled words in English.

questions.stem: Which sentence has a spelling mistake? If all three are correct, choose “No mistakes.”
options: The necessary forms are available in the front office.
It was an unusual occasion, so we took a picture.
He apologized without being asked.
No mistakes
questions.explanation: All three are correct. Necessary takes one c and two s's, and occasion takes two c's and one s.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence that demonstrates correct usage.
options: Me and Devin volunteered to carry the equipment.
Neither the coach nor the players was ready for the announcement.
The team celebrated their victory, they had trained all summer.
Each of the runners brought his or her own water bottle.
questions.explanation: Each is singular, so the singular pronoun is right. The others fail in three different ways: with neither/nor the verb agrees with players, the second is a comma splice and the fourth uses the object form Me as a subject.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence that demonstrates correct usage.
options: Their going to announce the winners after lunch.
Walking through the museum, the paintings seemed to glow.
The principal spoke to Marisol and I about the schedule change.
She could have finished sooner if the printer had worked.
questions.explanation: Could have is the correct form. The others use I where the object me is needed, dangle a modifier so the paintings appear to be walking and write Their for They're.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence that demonstrates correct usage.
options: The hikers left earlier than we did.
Everyone on the debate team have finished their research.
The letter was wrote by my grandmother in 1962.
If I would have known, I would have brought an umbrella.
questions.explanation: The comparison is complete and the subject pronoun we is correct before did. The others use a plural verb with the singular Everyone, use the past tense wrote where the participle written belongs and put would have in an if clause that needs had.

questions.stem: Choose the sentence that demonstrates correct usage.
options: Laying on the couch, Owen watched the storm move in.
Us students raised almost 400 dollars for the food drive.
She hardly never misses a practice.
The committee has not yet decided where it will meet.
questions.explanation: A committee acting as one body takes a singular verb. The others confuse laying with lying, use Us as a subject and pile hardly onto never for a double negative.

questions.stem: Choose the best word to join the thoughts together. Nadia had studied the map for an hour, ______ she still took a wrong turn at the second intersection.
options: whenever
therefore
yet
since
questions.explanation: The second clause contradicts what the first would lead you to expect, so a contrast word is needed. Since and therefore both signal cause, and whenever signals repetition.

questions.stem: Choose the best word to join the thoughts together. The gym will stay open late on Thursday ______ the district tournament begins that weekend.
options: or
because
whereas
but
questions.explanation: The tournament is the reason for the late hours. Whereas and but both set up a contrast that does not exist here, and or offers an alternative.

questions.stem: Choose the best word to join the thoughts together. You may keep the library book for another two weeks ______ no one else has requested it.
options: provided that
whenever
unless
although
questions.explanation: The extension depends on a condition being met, which is what provided that expresses. Unless reverses the condition, although makes it a concession and whenever makes it repeat.

questions.stem: Choose the best word to join the thoughts together. The volunteers had already filled every sandbag ______ the second truck arrived at the levee.
options: because
so that
in case
by the time
questions.explanation: Had already filled signals that one event was finished before the other, which calls for a time marker. Because and so that give reasons, and in case points to a possibility rather than to something that happened.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes this sentence. The museum guide gave a ______ account of the fire, mentioning the exact minute each alarm sounded.
options: polished
meticulous
lengthy
brisk
questions.explanation: The detail about exact minutes points to care and precision rather than to speed, length or polish. All four could describe a good account, so the sentence itself has to decide it.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes this sentence. Ms. Ferrara is a ______ reader; she finishes two novels most weekends.
options: voracious
careful
patient
skilled
questions.explanation: The clue is how much she reads, not how well. Careful, patient and skilled are all praise, but they describe the quality of her reading rather than its appetite.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes this sentence. The coach's instructions were so ______ that not one player had to ask a follow-up question.
options: forceful
brief
explicit
encouraging
questions.explanation: Nothing was left to ask, so the instructions must have spelled everything out. Forceful describes delivery, encouraging describes tone and brief instructions often produce more questions, not fewer.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best completes this sentence. Although the two paintings were made 200 years apart, the resemblance between them was ______ enough that the curators hung them side by side.
options: pleasant
modest
striking
curious
questions.explanation: Hanging the paintings together is a strong response, so the resemblance has to be strong. Modest points the other way, and pleasant and curious describe how the likeness feels rather than how obvious it is.

questions.stem: Which of these expresses the idea most clearly?
options: It was by the fifth graders that the recycling program at our school was started.
Our school's recycling program was started by the fifth graders.
The fifth graders started our school's recycling program.
Started by the fifth graders, our school's recycling program came into being.
questions.explanation: All four are grammatical, but only one puts the doers first and states the action directly. The rest bury the subject in a passive or in an It was construction.

questions.stem: Which of these expresses the idea most clearly?
options: Officials postponed the game because someone saw lightning.
The reason that the game was postponed was because of the fact that lightning was seen.
Lightning having been seen, the game was postponed.
The game was postponed due to the sighting of lightning.
questions.explanation: The clearest version names who acted and why in plain words. The others pad the idea with the reason was because of the fact, an awkward participial opening or a noun phrase where a verb belongs.

questions.stem: Which of these expresses the idea most clearly?
options: On the roof of the library is where a beehive is kept by Mr. Alvarez.
A beehive is kept on the library roof by Mr. Alvarez.
Mr. Alvarez keeps a beehive on the roof of the library.
There is a beehive that Mr. Alvarez keeps on the roof of the library.
questions.explanation: Subject, verb and object in order, with nothing added. The other three invert the sentence, make it passive or open with the empty There is.

questions.stem: Which of these expresses the idea most clearly?
options: What the storm did was knock down three of the oldest trees in the park.
The storm knocked down three of the park's oldest trees.
Three of the park's oldest trees were knocked down by the storm.
It was three of the park's oldest trees that the storm knocked down.
questions.explanation: The storm is the actor, so the storm belongs in the subject position. The other versions are correct English but reach the same idea through a passive or through an emphasis construction that adds words without adding meaning.

questions.stem: Which sentence does not belong in the paragraph? (1) A returning honeybee tells the rest of the hive where it found food by dancing on the comb. (2) The angle of the dance points the other bees toward the flowers, and the length of the waggle tells them how far to fly. (3) A single hive can produce more than 60 pounds of honey in a good summer. (4) Bees that watch the dance leave the hive and fly almost directly to the patch the dancer described.
options: Sentence 3
Sentence 1
Sentence 4
Sentence 2
questions.explanation: The paragraph is about how the dance carries information. Honey output is a fact about the same hive, so it is on topic, but it does nothing for the point being made.

questions.stem: Which sentence does not belong in the paragraph? (1) Before the Erie Canal opened, hauling a ton of flour from Buffalo to New York City by wagon cost roughly 100 dollars. (2) Thousands of laborers spent eight years digging the channel by hand. (3) Once barges could make the trip, the same ton moved for a small fraction of that price. (4) Farmers who had never been able to afford the wagon rate could suddenly sell their wheat in the city.
options: Sentence 3
Sentence 2
Sentence 4
Sentence 1
questions.explanation: Sentences 1, 3 and 4 trace the fall in shipping cost and what it made possible. How the canal was built belongs to the canal's story but not to this paragraph's argument about price.

questions.stem: Which sentence does not belong in the paragraph? (1) A Fresnel lens is built from dozens of glass rings set in a frame around a single lamp. (2) Each ring bends the light that strikes it toward the center, so rays that would have scattered into the sky are turned toward the horizon instead. (3) The result is a beam a ship's crew can see 20 miles out from a lamp no brighter than a household bulb. (4) Most American lighthouses were automated in the 20th century, and their keepers were reassigned.
options: Sentence 2
Sentence 1
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
questions.explanation: The paragraph explains how the lens concentrates light. Automation is a genuine fact about lighthouses, but it belongs to their history rather than to the mechanism described here.

questions.stem: Choose the pair of sentences that best develops this topic sentence. Topic sentence: A public library is worth more to a small town than its book collection suggests.
options: The library was built in 1911 with money left by a local banker. Its reading room still has the original oak tables.
Reading is one of the best habits a person can build. People who read regularly tend to have larger vocabularies.
The shelves hold about 12,000 volumes, and roughly a third of them are children's books. New titles arrive every month from a distributor in the state capital.
The building is one of the few places where anyone can sit all afternoon without buying something. Its meeting room hosts job workshops, tax help and the town council's open hearings.
questions.explanation: The topic sentence promises value beyond the books, so the development has to name that other value. The second pair describes the collection itself, which is the very thing the topic sentence sets aside, and the last two drift into general praise of reading and into the building's history.

questions.stem: Choose the pair of sentences that best develops this topic sentence. Topic sentence: Learning to cook a few basic meals changes how a teenager eats.
options: A student who can make eggs, rice and a simple soup stops depending on whatever is fastest to unwrap. Dinner becomes a decision instead of whatever is left in the freezer.
Restaurant meals are usually more expensive than meals made at home. A family of four can spend 60 dollars on one dinner out.
Kitchens can be dangerous places for beginners. Knives and hot pans cause thousands of injuries every year.
Chefs train for years before they are trusted with a professional kitchen. Most begin by chopping vegetables for someone else.
questions.explanation: The claim is about the teenager's own eating, so the pair has to show the change in what and how that student eats. Cost, professional training and kitchen safety are all about cooking, but none of them develops this claim.

questions.stem: Choose the pair of sentences that best develops this topic sentence. Topic sentence: The best time to see a meteor shower is in the hours just before dawn.
options: Cities make meteors hard to see because streetlights wash out everything but the brightest streaks. Driving 30 minutes out of town can double the number you count.

After midnight the side of Earth you are standing on has turned to face the direction of our orbit, so it sweeps up meteors head-on. Before midnight you are on the trailing side, and only the fastest particles can catch up.
Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through dust left behind by a comet. The dust burns up about 50 miles above the ground.
The Perseid shower returns every August and is the most watched of the year. Some observers count 60 meteors in an hour at its peak.
questions.explanation: The topic sentence is a claim about timing, and only one pair explains why the hour matters. The pair about city lights is about where to watch, which is a different question that is easy to mistake for support.

questions.stem: Which of these sentences offers the least support to the topic? Topic: Middle schools should start the day later than 7:30 a.m.
options: Districts that moved their first bell to 8:30 reported fewer tardies and better attendance.
Most middle schools serve breakfast in the cafeteria before the first bell.
Buses can run the elementary route first and the middle school route second without adding a single vehicle.
Teenagers' internal clocks shift during adolescence, so most cannot fall asleep before about 11 p.m.
questions.explanation: The first three give a biological reason, evidence from districts that tried it and an answer to the obvious objection about buses. Breakfast service is part of the school morning but says nothing about when the day should begin.

questions.stem: Which of these sentences offers the least support to the topic? Topic: Every student should learn to swim.
options: Drowning is one of the leading causes of accidental death for children under 15.
A swimmer who panics in deep water can float on her back until help arrives, and that skill takes one afternoon to teach.
Competitive swimmers train before school, often arriving at the pool by five in the morning.
Swimming is a low-impact exercise a person can keep doing into old age.
questions.explanation: The topic is about every student learning a basic skill. The training schedule of competitive swimmers is about swimming, but it describes a small group of specialists and gives no reason for the general claim.

questions.stem: Which of these sentences offers the least support to the topic? Topic: Cities should plant more trees along their streets.
options: Property values on tree-lined blocks run higher than on identical blocks without them.
Sugar maples reach their brightest color about two weeks earlier than the oaks planted beside them.
A street shaded by mature trees can be ten degrees cooler in August than a bare one a block away.
Tree roots pull rainwater out of the storm system, so heavy rain floods fewer intersections.
questions.explanation: Heat, flooding and property values are all reasons to plant. When one species changes color is a fact about street trees that gives a city no reason to plant more of them.
